title: The Airship Dock in the Sky
voice_direction: Daniel (onwK4e9ZLuTAKqWW03F9), steady British broadcaster at an unhurried pace; a dry smile on 'Some say that was the point', let 'wind' land alone after the pause, a touch of tension on the rope tearing free, then warm and settled on the last line.
narration: The Empire State Building's spire was built for airships. In nineteen twenty-nine, Al Smith announced a mooring mast for zeppelins. Passengers would walk down a gangplank, nearly a quarter mile up. [wry] It also out-climbed the Chrysler Building. Some say that was the point. [pause] One problem: wind. Updrafts hit the walls, and a ship tied by its nose can tip on end. In September nineteen thirty-one, a small airship touched the mast for about three minutes. A blimp tried to pick up mail. The rope tore free. The only delivery, reports say, was a bundle of newspapers. But the mast found another job. That December, NBC began experimental television broadcasts there. Today, New York stations still broadcast from the top. It was built to catch airships. [pause] It ended up sending voices into the air.

The top of the Empire State Building was built as a dock for airships 🎈 The only airship to touch it stayed about three minutes.

Would you have walked that gangplank? 👇

instagram_caption:
In December 1929, Al Smith, the former New York governor fronting the Empire State Building, announced that its top would be a mooring mast for airships. Passengers would step off a zeppelin and down a gangplank, nearly a quarter of a mile above Fifth Avenue.

The mast added about two hundred feet and lifted the tower to 1,250 feet, comfortably above the Chrysler Building's 1,046. Some historians think the height was the real point.

Then there was the wind. Updrafts race up the walls of a tall building, and an airship tied only by its nose has no ground crew to hold its tail. In 1927 a gust stood the Navy airship Los Angeles almost on end at a mast in New Jersey.

In September 1931 a small, privately owned airship touched the mast for about three minutes in strong wind, the New York Times reported. On 30 September the Goodyear blimp Columbia tried to collect two bags of mail; after a dozen passes, the rope tore out of a worker's hands. The only delivery, reports say, was a bundle of newspapers lowered on a rope.

But the mast found another job. On 22 December 1931 NBC began experimental television broadcasts from the building. A TV antenna went up on top in 1950, and New York radio and TV stations still broadcast from it today.

Would you have walked that gangplank? 👇

facts.claim: In December 1929 (11 December), Al Smith announced the Empire State Building would carry a mooring mast for dirigibles, raising its planned height to 1,250 feet
facts.source: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Docking on the Empire State Building'; American Heritage, 'A Chase Up Into the Sky' (Oct 1968, vol. 19 no. 6)

facts.claim: The plan: airships would moor at the mast and passengers would go down a gangplank to the building (reported in the New York Times, 1929)
facts.source: Smithsonian Air & Space (citing NYT); Museum of the City of New York blog, 'Doomed Dirigible Dock'

facts.claim: The mast put the Empire State Building (1,250 ft) above the Chrysler Building (1,046 ft with its secretly built spire); the height race is widely seen as a motive, though Smith publicly denied rivalry
facts.source: American Heritage, 'A Chase Up Into the Sky' (1968); Britannica, 'Empire State Building'

facts.claim: Hugo Eckener (Graf Zeppelin) called the scheme impractical: airship landings needed dozens of ground crew and plenty of rope, and a ship moored at the mast would be held only by its nose, with no ground lines; winds and updrafts at the top made holding position hard
facts.source: Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Docking on the Empire State Building'

facts.claim: 25 August 1927: a gust lifted the tail of USS Los Angeles moored at the Lakehurst high mast to a near-vertical position; minor damage, but it showed the risks of high mooring masts
facts.source: Naval Historical Center photo captions NH 84566-84568 (Online Library of Selected Images)

facts.claim: In September 1931 a privately owned dirigible made contact with the mast for about three minutes in a strong (about 40 mph) wind; the NYT named the pilot and reported traffic below tied up
facts.source: Smithsonian Air & Space (citing the New York Times, 1931); History.com, '10 Surprising Facts About the Empire State Building' ('tethered itself to the spire for a few minutes'). Some sources instead name the Navy blimp J-4, so the narration says only 'a small airship'

facts.claim: 30 September 1931: the Goodyear-Zeppelin blimp Columbia tried to pick up two bags of mail from the mast for the liner President Harding; after a dozen passes its rope reached one man (Andrew Kelly) and tore out of his grasp
facts.source: Library of Congress, New York World-Telegram & Sun photo caption, 'Blimp takes mail from Empire State Building - almost'

facts.claim: A blimp lowered a bundle of newspapers (reportedly the Evening Journal) to the mast on a rope; the only 'delivery' the mast ever handled. Hedged in narration ('reports say') because accounts differ on date and sequence
facts.source: History.com; Museum of the City of New York blog 'Doomed Dirigible Dock'; Smithsonian Air & Space

facts.claim: No airship ever moored there to board or unload passengers; the mast was soon used for broadcasting
NBC (with RCA, which leased the 85th floor) began experimental television transmissions from the first Empire State antenna on 22 December 1931 (W2XF vision, W2XK sound)
facts.source: Broadcast Engineering (1967), 'Broadcast Antennas on the Empire State Building', reprinted at tech-notes.tv / lnl.com; Telos Alliance blog 'The Empire State Building: Where It All Began'

facts.claim: A 222-foot television antenna mast was added in 1950, bringing the total height to 1,472 ft (1,454 ft after the 1985 replacement)
New York FM and TV stations still transmit from the Empire State Building's master antennas (Radio World reports 15 FMs on the master FM antenna plus TV stations including WABC-TV and WPIX)
facts.source: Radio World, 'Empire State Building Climbers Force NYC FM and TV Stations to Backup Antennas'
